source.title: Turning Abliteration into Model Self-Destruction in Open-Weight LLMs

page_placements.theme: Robustness to direction-based removal: training against ablation, decoys, hidden switches, and removal routes that bypass the direction

record.file_problem: None; the text contains the paper and appendices through the end. Some appendix references are written as “Appendix ??” in the paper.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies difference-in-means abliteration and an adaptive ablation attack, then reports their effects on refusal, harmful-output attack success, and perplexity. This tests the removal and practical-removal claims, but uses its own attack setup and HarmBench ASR rather than reproducing the full original intervention and measure.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports clean LAMBADA scores before and after its defense training; these measure the cost of training the defense, not capability after abliteration, so they are not separate rows. The cited results from other papers are not recorded as findings here.
record.test_reason: Most of the paper reports its own defense's performance, which is T4-like. It also runs difference-in-means abliteration on two undefended stock checkpoints through the same pipeline and reports HarmBench ASR. Those controls (0.72 Llama-3.1-8B, 0.56 Gemma-2-27B, Sections 5.1 and 5.3) are its own results on whether ablating the direction removes refusal in released models. The measure (HarmBench ASR) and the single-layer attack differ from the original. The defended-model results measure a deliberately trained defense, not the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that simulating refusal-subspace ablation during training can make that edit fail to yield a capable uncensored model. Standard abliteration falls to 0.00 ASR on all 8 models; the adaptive attack is mitigated on 6 of 8, with residual Qwen-family vulnerability and a clear failure on Qwen-2.5-72B. They add that defended numbers are optimistic because defended runs used refusal-only attack selection, and that no robustness to fine-tuning or arbitrary tampering is claimed.
record.recipe_differences: The study applies difference-in-means abliteration and adaptive ablation, but attacks at selected layers or through a simplified search rather than projecting the direction out of every layer and position. It reports HarmBench ASR, refusal, and perplexity; it does not test adding the direction to harmless prompts. Its main contribution is a new robustness-training procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome depends on model family and size, standard versus adaptive attack, refusal-survival band placement, and attack-selection criterion. The paper reports that changing the band improves Gemma-2-27B but worsens Gemma-2-9B, and that fluency-gated selection materially changes undefended attack success.

fits_no_version.finding: Training against simulated ablation in a refusal subspace makes standard abliteration yield 0.00 ASR on all 8 defended models. On 5 models perplexity explodes (collapse); on Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen-2.5-72B refusal stays at 1.00 and 0.97 with fluent output.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Deliberate training against direction ablation can make difference-in-means ablation fail to produce a capable non-refusing model, via either collapse or persistent refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: Despite that defense, an adaptive single-layer mean-aggregation direction ablation still fluently jailbreaks Qwen-2.5-72B (refusal 0.08, ppl 3.5, ASR 0.77; 0.72 after retraining). Qwen-7B/32B keep 0.25/0.19 ASR, while Llama and Gemma stay at 0.00–0.06.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In some model families a removable refusal direction survives training aimed at eliminating it; removability is family-dependent.

fits_no_version.finding: Refusal-survival band placement trades off against the collapse trigger in opposite ways on Gemma-2-9B and Gemma-2-27B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Collapse and refusal-persistence objectives compete for the same primary refusal direction, with the outcome depending on model size.

record.peer_reviewed: preprint; under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027
record.problems: ASR, refusal, and over-refusal are evaluated on 100 held-out prompts; LAMBADA uses a 300-example subset. Each model is trained once, with no seed variance reported. ASR uses one classifier. The paper acknowledges that defended results use refusal-only attack selection while undefended controls use fluency-gated selection, and says a like-for-like rerun is outstanding. The adaptive attack searches single-layer ablations and is described as weaker than the full Heretic tool.
record.rows_left_out: Clean LAMBADA before/after defense-training results are not rows because they do not measure capability after abliteration. No other claim-relevant numeric results were omitted.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to harmless prompts to induce refusal. Refusal rate and capability (perplexity, LAMBADA) after ablation on undefended models are not reported numerically. Ablation across all layers and positions is not tested. Only two stock models are used.
Whether the attack is applied as a persistent weight edit versus inference-time projection is not stated. Publicly released abliterated models are not evaluated.
Not tested. Prompt-based jailbreaks are not evaluated, and robustness from training against ablation is measured only against ablation attacks.
Original refusal training is not varied. The defense training changes removability on purpose, which is recorded under fits_no_version.

record.verdict_notes: The claim-relevant evidence is limited to the undefended controls (r17, r18, r56–r58). Table 2's 'Clean' column is post-defense, not stock. The adaptive attack is a simplified, single-layer analogue of Heretic. Undefended and defended runs use different attack-selection criteria. Each model is trained once with 100 eval prompts and no seed variance. The paper is dated ICLR 2027 under review, and its reference to models such as Kimi-K3 cannot be checked.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test adding the direction to harmless prompts. Its undefended ablation controls are reported for only two models; its ablation attacks do not project the direction out of every layer and position.
Does not test every released model or every weight-edit procedure. The defended-model results use a refusal-only attack-selection criterion, while undefended controls use a fluency gate.
Does not test other jailbreak families or establish that all attacks work by suppressing this direction. The authors do not claim robustness to fine-tuning or other weight modifications.
Does not compare affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts of refusal against a single-direction account.
Does not separately measure harmfulness judgments and refusal decisions.
Does not test transfer across languages, base/instruct variants, or model variants of a shared checkpoint.
Tests different defense-training configurations, but does not test when refusal was originally trained or whether that determines the existence of one removable direction.

tranche.reason: It runs single-layer DIM abliteration, judged by HarmBench, on undefended stock checkpoints as controls (0.72, 0.56) and shows a selection-criterion artifact. That is its own result on the claim with a method different from the original's. It also directly tests training against ablation.

source_check.notes: Pack verdicts had no [lN] ids; l1-l4 follow listed order. Defended rows r01-r16, r49, r50, r55 link to V3 but no V3 verdict exists, though the study tests training against ablation on 7B-72B; their conditions omit refusal-only selection, which the authors call optimistic (App. H). Text inconsistencies: Sec 5.1 says adaptive attack mitigated on 7/8, Fig 1 and Conclusion say 6/8; Table 2 Gemma-2-27B adaptive refusal 0.99 conflicts with App. G; defended Qwen-2.5-7B (ppl 6.4, ref 0.01, ASR 0.00) fits neither defense mode. ICLR reviewer-policy footer addresses humans, not an injection.

statements.correction: Defended, standard abliteration: ASR 0.00 on all 8. On 5 models refusal falls to 0.00-0.04 while benign ppl rises to 1.7x10^4-3.4x10^8 (collapse); Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen-2.5-72B keep refusal at 1.00 and 0.97. Adaptive ASR: Qwen-2.5-7B 0.25, Qwen-2.5-32B 0.19, Qwen-2.5-72B 0.77 (0.72 after retraining). Defended runs used refusal-only selection; undefended controls used fluency-gated selection (App. H).
statements.problem: The numbers are right, but 'resist the edit' leaves out three things. The adaptive attack beats the defended Qwen-2.5-72B and partly beats the defended Qwen 7B/32B. Five models 'resist' only by collapsing. The authors call the defended figures optimistic because the selection criterion differs.

statements.correction: Standard abliteration ASR 0.00 on 8 defended instruct models, 7B-72B: Llama-3.1-8B/70B, Qwen-2.5-7B/32B/72B, Gemma-1-7B, Gemma-2-9B/27B (rows r01-r08). Adaptive attack: Qwen-2.5-72B 0.77.

Accurate: 0.00 on 8, ppl explodes on 5, and Qwen-2.5-72B at refusal 0.08, ppl 3.5, ASR 0.77 (0.72 retrained). Llama/Gemma adaptive 0.00-0.06. The 'unfit' placement is doubtful because this is training against ablation (V3).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Undefended Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-27B under fluency-gated standard abliteration
reader_labels.reason: The reported attack-success rates are 0.72 and 0.56, respectively, after difference-in-means abliteration (r17–r18).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Defended instruction-tuned models under standard and adaptive ablation
reader_labels.reason: Several models retain refusal or fail to produce harmful outputs after removal, while others show low refusal only alongside collapse; these results concern defended models and do not establish the original claim across stock models (r01–r16, r19–r50).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Undefended stock Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-27B under fluency-gated abliteration
reader_labels.reason: The attacks achieve ASR 0.72 and 0.56, respectively (r17–r18).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Defended models, adaptive attacks, and the reported attack-selection protocol
reader_labels.reason: The defense reduces standard-attack ASR to 0.00 in its reported runs, but adaptive results vary substantially by model, and the paper notes that defended and undefended results use different selection criteria (r01–r16, r55–r58).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Standard abliteration after the study’s robustness training
reader_labels.reason: Standard abliteration produces ASR 0.00 on all eight defended models in the reported configuration (r01–r08).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Adaptive abliteration and model-specific defense configurations
reader_labels.reason: Adaptive attacks retain nonzero ASR on Qwen models and strongly defeat Qwen-2.5-72B; changing refusal-survival bands also helps one Gemma model but hurts another (r10, r12–r16, r51–r55).
